turns.question: Our sonde spits out a number in uS/cm for salt. I get the microsiemens part, but what is the 'per centimetre' actually doing there - is that a reading divided by something, or a property of the water itself?
turns.answer:
The "per centimetre" reflects that conductivity is a property of the water itself, not just a raw reading. Electrical conductivity is "a measure of the electrical conductance (G) of a substance normalized to a unit length and cross-sectional area" 【14†"a measure of the electrical conductance (G) of a substance normalized to a unit length and cross-sectional area"】.

In other words, the meter measures a conductance between two electrode plates, and the instrument converts it using the cell constant — "the ratio of the distance between two electrode plates (d) and their area (A)" 【14†"the ratio of the distance between two electrode plates (d) and their area (A)"】 — so the result describes the water's intrinsic ability to carry current, independent of the particular probe geometry. That's why the units come out as siemens per centimetre, most commonly reported as microsiemens per centimetre (μS/cm) at 25 °C 【7†"The USGS typically reports the electrical conductivity of water as specific conductance in units of microsiemens per centimetre (μS/cm) at 25 °C."】.

So it's not your reading divided by something after the fact — it's the water's conductance normalized through the probe's cell constant (κ = K_cell × G) 【14†"where 𝐾cell is the cell constant (in units of cm-1)"】.

1.1 Overview of Specific Conductance
Specific conductance is an indirect measure of the collec-
tive concentration of dissolved ions in solution, and is defined
as the electrical conductance of 1 cubic centimeter (cm³) of a
solution at 25 degrees Celsius (°C) (Hem, 1982). The terms
“specific conductance,” “specific electrical conductance,” and
“electrical conductivity” have been used interchangeably in
the literature to report the same measurement. Because the
term “electrical conductivity” is not always referenced to a
standard temperature, the measurement or reference tempera-
ture must be reported with this parameter. The USGS National
Water Information System (NWIS) reports the measurement
of electrical conductance as specific conductance at 25 °C,
meaning that at any temperature for which the measurement
is made, the value is corrected to what it would be at 25 ºC.
The term “specific conductance” is correctly defined as the
electrical conductance of 1 cm³ of a solution at 25 °C. If the
electrical conductance is measured at another temperature, the
value is corrected to what it would be at 25 °C and reported as
specific conductance at 25 °C. Most modern specific con-
ductance meters are temperature compensated and report the
corrected value automatically.
The term “specific conductance” is correctly defined as the
electrical conductance of 1 cubic centimeter of a solution at
25 °C. If the electrical conductance is measured at another
temperature, the value is corrected to what it would be at
25 °C and reported as specific conductance at 25 °C.
In aqueous solutions, electrical conductance (G, measured
in siemens [S]) is the inverse of electrical resistance (R,
measured in ohms [Ω]), and is the capacity of water to conduct
an electric current as a result of the movement of ions through
the solution. Electrical conductivity (κ) is a measure of the
electrical conductance (G) of a substance normalized to a unit
length and cross-sectional area.

Maintenance

The "per centimetre" reflects that conductivity is a property of the water itself, not just a raw reading. Electrical conductivity is "a measure of the electrical conductance (G) of a substance normalized to a unit length and cross-sectional area" 【14†"a measure of the electrical conductance (G) of a substance normalized to a unit length and cross-sectional area"】.

In other words, the meter measures a conductance between two electrode plates, and the instrument converts it using the cell constant — "the ratio of the distance between two electrode plates (d) and their area (A)" 【14†"the ratio of the distance between two electrode plates (d) and their area (A)"】 — so the result describes the water's intrinsic ability to carry current, independent of the particular probe geometry. That's why the units come out as siemens per centimetre, most commonly reported as microsiemens per centimetre (μS/cm) at 25 °C 【7†"The USGS typically reports the electrical conductivity of water as specific conductance in units of microsiemens per centimetre (μS/cm) at 25 °C."】.

So it's not your reading divided by something after the fact — it's the water's conductance normalized through the probe's cell constant (κ = K_cell × G) 【14†"where 𝐾cell is the cell constant (in units of cm-1)"】.

turns.question: Someone dug up a survey of the same creek from decades back and every salt number in it is written in micromhos per centimetre. Do we have to convert those before we can put them next to ours?
turns.answer:
No conversion needed — micromhos per centimetre and microsiemens per centimetre are the same unit under different names. The USGS manual notes that "The units of electrical conductivity are siemens per centimeter (S/cm), which is the equivalent of mhos per centimeter (mhos/cm)" 【8†"The units of electrical conductivity are siemens per centimeter (S/cm), which is the equivalent of mhos per centimeter (mhos/cm)."】. It also mentions that "Most values reported prior to 1971 were in units of mhos per centimeter" 【8†"Most values reported prior to 1971 were in units of mhos per centimeter."】 — which fits the age of your survey.

So you can put those old micromhos/cm values directly alongside your μS/cm readings. One caveat from the same source: the measurement or reference temperature should be reported with the parameter 【8†"the measurement or reference temperature must be reported with this parameter"】, so it's worth checking whether the old survey states the temperature its values are referenced to.

1.1 Overview of Specific Conductance
Specific conductance is an indirect measure of the collec-
tive concentration of dissolved ions in solution, and is defined
as the electrical conductance of 1 cubic centimeter (cm³) of a
solution at 25 degrees Celsius (°C) (Hem, 1982). The terms
“specific conductance,” “specific electrical conductance,” and
“electrical conductivity” have been used interchangeably in
the literature to report the same measurement. Because the
term “electrical conductivity” is not always referenced to a
standard temperature, the measurement or reference tempera-
ture must be reported with this parameter. The USGS National
Water Information System (NWIS) reports the measurement
of electrical conductance as specific conductance at 25 °C,
meaning that at any temperature for which the measurement
is made, the value is corrected to what it would be at 25 ºC.
The term “specific conductance” is correctly defined as the
electrical conductance of 1 cm³ of a solution at 25 °C. If the
electrical conductance is measured at another temperature, the
value is corrected to what it would be at 25 °C and reported as
specific conductance at 25 °C. Most modern specific con-
ductance meters are temperature compensated and report the
corrected value automatically.
The term “specific conductance” is correctly defined as the
electrical conductance of 1 cubic centimeter of a solution at
25 °C. If the electrical conductance is measured at another
temperature, the value is corrected to what it would be at
25 °C and reported as specific conductance at 25 °C.
In aqueous solutions, electrical conductance (G, measured
in siemens [S]) is the inverse of electrical resistance (R,
measured in ohms [Ω]), and is the capacity of water to conduct
an electric current as a result of the movement of ions through
the solution. Electrical conductivity (κ) is a measure of the
electrical conductance (G) of a substance normalized to a unit
length and cross-sectional area.

The USGS manual notes that "The units of electrical conductivity are siemens per centimeter (S/cm), which is the equivalent of mhos per centimeter (mhos/cm)" 【8†"The units of electrical conductivity are siemens per centimeter (S/cm), which is the equivalent of mhos per centimeter (mhos/cm)."】.
